Roman Anthony is out of the Boston Red Sox lineup, raising an immediate question about whether something is wrong with the young star.
Here’s why Anthony is out of the lineup and what his absence means for the Red Sox.
Anthony is out of the Boston Red Sox lineup Thursday against Cleveland, but the club has not attached any new injury news to the decision.
Thursday is Anthony’s first day off since he returned from the injured list. The Red Sox have just three regular-season games left to play after Thursday.

Roman Anthony’s Lineup Status for Guardians Series Finale
Manager Chad Tracy had not yet explained the absence when the club posted the lineup ahead of his pregame media session.
The rest of the card shows how the night is built. Jarren Duran starts in left field, Mickey Gasper takes the designated hitter spot and Ceddanne Rafaela returns to center. Gasper bats right-handed, and Cleveland counters with right-hander Daniel Espino, according to MLB.com‘s lineup page. Left-hander Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) starts for Boston.
Rafaela left Wednesday’s 1-0 win with right hamstring tightness and was set to undergo an MRI Thursday, according to the Boston Globe. Duran replaced Rafaela in the third inning and went 2-for-3, according to the Globe‘s recap. Willson Contreras sits again.
Gasper was among the players optioned to make room for Anthony’s return.
“It was bittersweet. Like, I really mean it,” Tracy said, as quoted by Yahoo Sports.
Boston has already clinched a playoff spot. Tuesday’s card benched Trevor Story, Duran and Contreras with no public explanation, according to NESN reporter Rodney Knuppel.

Boston Red Sox Playoff Plans for Roman Anthony
No report ties Thursday’s absence to the right ring finger that cost Anthony nearly four months. He left a May 4 game at Detroit with wrist and hand discomfort, later described as a partially torn ligament, according to NESN‘s injury timeline.
Rehab stalled. Anthony “hasn’t made any substantive progress,” Tracy said in a late-June update, as quoted by Boston.com.
The Red Sox shifted him to the 60-day list and sent him to Fort Myers. Even after 3 1/2 months, the club declined to circle a return date, according to the Boston Globe. He was finally activated on Aug. 30, according to NBC Sports.
He has hit .242/.294/.432 with four home runs in 22 games since activation. His return began 10-for-22 over five games, then cooled to .137/.214/.296 across 56 plate appearances through Sept. 18. That night at Tampa Bay he hit a 438-foot leadoff homer, according to CBS Sports. He went 0-for-5 Tuesday and 1-for-4 Wednesday, according to CBS Sports‘ game log.
Tracy has resisted singling out Anthony during cold stretches.
“It’s not a Roman thing,” he said in May, as quoted by The Boston Globe.
Anthony wants the October he missed in 2025 with an oblique injury, and he said he is “where I want to be,” as quoted by The Boston Globe. The AL wild-card series opens Tuesday.
Anthony remains active and available off the bench. Any appearance Thursday would likely come as a pinch hitter, a role for his left-handed bat late in the game.

The Red Sox have secured a postseason berth. Now they need their offense to look ready for October. Boston enters Wednesday’s game against the Cleveland Guardians on a three-game losing streak. The Red Sox have scored two runs or fewer in each of those losses, putting more attention on the lineup Chad Tracy will send out against Cleveland left-hander Foster Griffin.
Jahmai Jones is batting third again, between Nick Sogard and Wilyer Abreu. Roman Anthony leads off, while Adley Rutschman bats fifth after collecting three hits, including two doubles, in Tuesday’s 3-2 loss.
The Red Sox announced Wednesday’s lineup ahead of the 7:10 p.m. ET game at Fenway Park.
Red Sox Lineup Vs. Guardians On Wednesday
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Nick Sogard, 1B
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Trevor Story, SS
- Andruw Monasterio, 2B
Sonny Gray will start for Boston against Griffin.

— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 23, 2026
Jones’ place in the order is worth watching. Batting him third puts a right-handed hitter between Sogard and Abreu against a left-handed starter. It also gives Jones another opportunity to strengthen his case for a significant postseason role.
Offense Needs To Step Up
Rutschman gave Boston one of its few bright spots Tuesday, but the Red Sox could not build enough offense around him. Mickey Gasper’s pinch-hit homer tied the game in the eighth inning before Cleveland pulled out the win. Boston has dropped five of its last seven games.
Gray enters Wednesday with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA. A strong outing from him would help stop the skid, but the Red Sox also need to see more from a lineup that has gone quiet at an uncomfortable time.
Boston is postseason-bound. Wednesday offers a chance to start playing like it.

This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more.
Ronald Acuña Jr. of the Braves may be hitting .259 with career lows in exit velocity and hard-hit rate, but don’t be fooled by the overall stats. If the star outfielder can fight through a left shin contusion he suffered Tuesday night on a foul ball at the plate—he’s currently considered day-to-day—he’ll be a force to be reckoned with in October. Ever since mid-August when Acuña began to knock off the rust from two IL stints, he’s been a dangerous, dynamic hitter.
The tell-tale sign is how Acuña is getting to high fastballs he used to miss.
| Acuna vs. 95+ MPH | No. | BA | SLG | HR | Attack Angle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Through Aug. 22 | 315 | .183 | .268 | 1 | 9° |
| Since | 119 | .393 | .857 | 4 | 7° |
Pitchers were dominating Acuña with velocity over his hands. No more. Acuña has made the adjustment. While his barrel had been working underneath the pitch plane, now he is flattening his attack angle, as you can see here:
Acuña heads my list of hitters who are most likely to cap a disappointing year with a strong finish.
Down Year but Primed for Big October
1. Ronald Acuña Jr., Braves
2. Mookie Betts, Dodgers
3. Will Smith, Dodgers
4. Trevor Story, Red Sox
5. José Ramírez, Guardians
Gerrit Cole, Game 2 Starter?
Yankees righthander Gerrit Cole broke through a late-season slump with an improved outing Friday in Arizona (six innings, two earned runs).
As I said last week here, Cole has been throwing too many strikes in the middle of the plate. His fix: tighten the delivery to be more compact and move almost six inches on the rubber toward the third base side.
A frequent tinkerer, Cole began the season toward the center of the rubber but after the Red Sox pounded him for four runs June 27, he moved to the first base side July 3 and stayed there for 13 starts. But after his poor start Sept. 12 against the Mets, which included a career high of hard hits, he returned to the center.
Here you can see his foot position change on the rubber in his past two starts:
It’s the quickest fix to a command issue. You don’t need to change mechanics, just the lane in which the ball leaves your hand.
How did it work? His command was much better. Look at his fastball heat maps and it’s clear he did a better job of keeping the ball out of the center lane:
Cole Fastball Heat Maps
This start moved Cole closer to getting the ball ahead of Max Fried or Carlos Rodon (or both) in a wild-card series against Boston.
As usual, Cole pounded the zone. He has not issued a walk among 71 batters faced in his past three starts. But still a concern: the swing-and-miss still has not returned to his game. He had only six swings-and-misses against Arizona. His September whiff rate is 17%, down from 22.4% entering the month.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have a difficult decision in choosing who starts after Schlittler, a decision that should be based on how Cole, Fried and Rodon are throwing the ball rather than sheer numbers or opponent trends. The Red Sox are slightly better against left-handed pitching (24–15, .746 OPS) than right-handed (60–55, .713 OPS), though the return of Roman Anthony changes that a bit.

The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

BOSTON -- When Payton Tolle walked off the mound with two outs in the top of the sixth inning on Tuesday night, it was the perfect opportunity for the Fenway faithful to recognize the power lefty for an outstanding rookie season.
Next time Tolle pitches, the noise is likely to be even louder, and not nearly as favorable.
The Red Sox will have no hesitation sending out the confident, charismatic 23-year-old into enemy territory.
While this was far from the best (5 2/3 innings, 8 hits, 2 ER, 2 BBs, 5 K’s) of Tolle’s 26 regular-season starts, it was more than enough to keep the Red Sox in the game.
Assuming Tolle doesn’t pitch again in the regular season, his final stat line includes this: A 3.03 ERA, 171 strikeouts, 40 walks, 1.10 WHIP and a .222 opponents batting average.
Playing short-handed without Willson Contreras (bruised knuckle, right hand), Ceddanne Rafaela (right quadriceps strain, 10-day IL) and Trevor Story (rest), the Red Sox continued their recent trend of not scoring much.
There were two bright spots.
Mickey Gasper came up as a pinch-hitter and hammered a game-tying solo shot to right in the bottom of the eighth.
Adley Rutschman, who had been slumping of late, belted two doubles as part of a three-hit night.

There were no guarantees on the night of April 25, when Chad Tracy was abruptly pulled from what ultimately became his 499th and final win as Triple-A Worcester manager, and handed the keys to Boston’s big-league kingdom on an interim basis.
Nor the next morning when Tracy, 41, walked into the Camden Yards visitors’ clubhouse in Baltimore to manage his first big-league game, to stunned and upset Red Sox players publicly questioning the future of the organization after the previous night’s firing of longtime manager Alex Cora and six coaches.
The future became clearer on Tuesday morning. Hours before opening the final homestand of 2026, and fresh off clinching a playoff spot for the second consecutive year, the Red Sox officially announced Tracy’s new three-year contract to become their 49th manager, and the exercising of their 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“When it became time to make the very difficult change in leadership with our major league team, there was kind of really only one name that was considered,” Breslow said as he, Tracy and team president and CEO Sam Kennedy sat in the Fenway Park interview room Tuesday afternoon to discuss the day’s news.
The Red Sox were 10-17, tied for the American League’s worst record, when Tracy arrived. And they got worse before they got better. They lost several stars to injuries in late April and early May, and fell to their worst home record to begin a season since 1932 in early June.
“I mean, it was abysmal,” Kennedy said. “April, May and June were brutal to live through.”
As the losses mounted, so did public perception of Tracy as a stalking horse, and Breslow as a man on borrowed time. But within the organization, Red Sox leadership and players felt a significant shift when Tracy took the reins.
“It became pretty clear early on that Chad was the right person at the right time to lead this group,” Breslow, 46, said. “(We) recognized that this was a fit we wanted to preserve. … I think there was probably some realization a few weeks ago, maybe even further, that there’s a natural conclusion here that we’re working toward.”
The question of Tracy’s future with the organization was present from the start, both internally and externally, but he remained unruffled.
“Yeah, I mean, it didn’t bother me much anyways,” Tracy said. “I worried about the players. I worried about getting us on track, helping get us on track. … That was what my focus was on, and I figured this stuff, if it goes well enough, it’ll come together on its own.”
Tracy took a similar approach to last offseason’s WooSox managerial contract negotiations. Many might try to make the leap to a major league coaching job after managing a Triple-A team to winning seasons in each of their four years at the helm, and spending over two decades playing and working in the minor leagues. But Tracy took the “Que Sera Sera” approach; whatever will be, will be.
“I think those opportunities happen on their own,” Tracy said. “You don’t operate in those jobs thinking about, how do I get to my next one? You just do your job. … I’m here to help people. I’m here to help the players. And if I do that properly, then whether it’s here or somewhere else, those things always take care of themselves.”
Tracy’s unbotheredness by limbo and chaos, and his ability to navigate turbulent waters and help his players do the same were key factors in the removal of the interim tag.
Asked what he learned about Tracy after moving him up to the majors, Breslow said, “The answer to that is maybe what makes Chad most remarkable, which is, he was exactly the same. He was exactly as he was as the manager in Worcester, he was exactly the same after a shutout win as he was a heart-wrenching defeat, and I think that stability, that consistency, is how our players have responded so well.
“So what I’ve learned is he is just an unbelievably intense but even-keeled leader, someone who builds sincere and authentic relationships with everyone that he interacts with and comes across, someone that I think can can be trusted to be honest and questioned when it’s appropriate to do so, and someone who is willing to always put the players in the organization first.”
Members of the Red Sox echoed Breslow’s sentiments.
“I’m happy for him, because he’s handled this amazingly,” veteran shortstop Trevor Story told the Herald. “Odds were kind of stacked against him, and kind of our team in general, too. So happy for him, and he deserves it. He stewarded the ship in an incredible way, so pumped for him that he can kick that interim tag and be here for a while.”
“He’s a real calming influence,” Story continued. “If you talk to him or get to know him at all, he’s very level-headed, really knowledgeable baseball guy, and just being around him is a good feeling. So that goes a long way, I think, to being a manager, and I think yeah, he’s shown that he can handle this whole situation of Boston and everything going on.”
“He’s done an incredible job, just bringing this clubhouse together, and just taking it one day at a time, and I am incredibly happy for him,” catcher and first baseman Mickey Gasper told the Herald. “There’s nobody that’s earned something more that I’ve been around in the game of baseball than Trace, getting this job. He’s done a tremendous job, and I couldn’t think of anybody else better for the role.”
“I’ve learned so much from him,” added Gasper, who played for Tracy on the ‘24 WooSox and split this season between Worcester and Boston. “How to be a baseball man around your teammates, how to bring a fresh slate every day to the ballpark.
“The wins and losses wear on you that day. Playing for Trace the last couple years, even in the minor leagues we’ve had some tough losses together, and he always comes back the next day. Today is a new day. This is the task at hand, and just being able to turn the page after tough spots, tough losses, just adversity in general. And I think just watching him go about his business that’s what I’ve learned the most. He leads by example.”
Those particular attributes also made Tracy an ideal partner for Breslow. The latter must make the difficult decisions, the former has proved adept at ensuring the ripple effects don’t become tsunamis. The Red Sox feel this pairing will provide the stability that has been in scarce supply over the last decade.
“It’s huge,” Kennedy said of locking in this tandem for the next three years. “It’s a sacred relationship, between the head of baseball operations and the manager. Being on the same page, having that trust, that confidence in each other (is) something that I’ve learned going back to my days at the New York Yankees and the San Diego Padres. And here, seeing successful versions of it, and seeing unsuccessful versions of it.
“Lord knows we’ve made mistakes in our time. And just ensuring that you have that relationship right is critical. So yeah, it’s great to have that stability now. And look, we haven’t achieved anything, we know that. But I think we’re set up for success going forward.”
Story was glad to say he felt differently than that morning in Baltimore, when he was one of several longtime Red Sox who wondered “what the true direction of the franchise is.”
“When AC and all the guys got let go, we didn’t know the direction,” Story said. “And now, I feel like we do.”

The Boston Red Sox have scored 2.82 runs per game across their last 11 outings. The lineup is collectively batting .210 and posting a .621 OPS in that span. Wilyer Abreu, Adley Rutschman, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Nick Sogard have all gone cold at the wrong time.
With the Wild Card Series beginning September 29, the Red Sox need their bats to wake up before October arrives.
The cavalry is coming. And the timing could not be better.
The Latest on Rafaela
Ceddanne Rafaela is expected to return to the lineup on Tuesday when the Red Sox open a three-game series against the Guardians at Fenway Park.
The All-Star center fielder has been sidelined for 16 games since straining his right quadriceps.
Chad Tracy indicated over the weekend that Rafaela should come off the injured list for the homestand. The rotation is set up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez, a sequence that mirrors how the staff could be deployed in the Wild Card Series.
Getting Rafaela back before those games begin gives him a chance to find his timing and reintegrate into the lineup before the stakes get higher.
What Rafaela Brings Back
Rafaela's absence has been felt. On the season, he has produced 16 home runs, 70 RBIs, and a .282/.760 line. His combination of contact, power, and speed makes him one of the most complete players on the roster.
The defensive impact is equally significant. Rafaela's range in center field changes the way the pitching staff operates. Fly balls that fall for hits with other outfielders become outs when he is patrolling the middle of the outfield. His presence there tightens the entire defense.
The Red Sox have been using Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton to fill the void in center. Both have been serviceable, but neither provides the combination of offense and defense that Rafaela delivers on a daily basis.
The Red Sox Offense Needs a Spark
The numbers paint a clear picture of how badly the Red Sox have struggled at the plate.
Mickey Gasper is 4-for-25 over the recent stretch. Kiner-Falefa has managed just one hit in his last 20 at-bats. Sogard is 8-for-40. The lineup has lacked the consistent production that fueled the summer surge.
There have been bright spots. Roman Anthony broke out of a prolonged slump with a 5-for-13 weekend against the Rays that included two doubles and a homer. Trevor Story has been one of the hottest hitters on the roster since returning from the injured list, carrying a .338 average with an .869 OPS across 19 games.
Willson Contreras is also working his way back from a bruised right hand and could return this week. If both Contreras and Rafaela rejoin the lineup for the Guardians series, it would be the healthiest the Red Sox' batting order has looked in weeks.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox have six games left before the playoffs begin.
Rafaela's return gives the lineup a jolt it needs. What he provides on both sides of the ball is invaluable for Boston.
Fenway awaits.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox did not clinch their postseason berth with a dramatic walk-off hit or a dominant performance from their pitching staff. They clinched after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays and receiving help from Mike Yastrzemski and the Atlanta Braves.
Interim manager Chad Tracy did not care how the ticket was punched.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” Tracy told reporters. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
That message perfectly captured Boston’s remarkable season. The Red Sox were 32-46 and appeared destined to spend the summer discussing trades, organizational changes and another disappointing finish. Instead, they became the first team in MLB history to finish above .500 and reach the playoffs after losing at least 46 of its first 78 games.
“They didn’t take no for an answer,” Tracy said.
Where It Started
Tracy inherited a 10-17 team when the Red Sox moved on from Alex Cora in April. There was no immediate transformation, and Boston’s season continued to drift for several weeks.
Eventually, everything changed. Boston swept four games from the New York Yankees at Fenway Park in late June and began one of the most impressive turnarounds in franchise history. Young players developed into meaningful contributors, the clubhouse remained together and the Red Sox kept finding ways to survive injuries.
The result is a second consecutive postseason appearance and another likely Wild Card Series against the Yankees. That matchup did not work out for Boston last October. The Red Sox won the opener behind Garrett Crochet but dropped the next two games in New York.
This year’s roster has traveled a much different road.
The Red Sox have played meaningful baseball for months because almost every loss threatened to undo the progress they had made. Players such as Roman Anthony, Payton Tolle and Connelly Early have grown up in that environment, while veterans including Trevor Story and Willson Contreras helped keep the clubhouse steady.
Getting Things Set Up
Now Boston has an opportunity to set its rotation, protect tired relievers and enter the postseason with more than a week to prepare. The final regular-season games still matter, especially with the Cleveland Guardians visiting Fenway Park. Boston can use the series to evaluate potential postseason matchups and determine which pitchers are best equipped for important October innings.
The celebration also strengthens Tracy’s case to remain manager beyond this season. Boston did not merely improve after he took control. The Red Sox completed a turnaround that had never been accomplished in major league history.
Tracy did not want credit Sunday. His message remained focused on the players who refused to allow a terrible start to define them. That approach may be one of the biggest reasons the Red Sox are still playing.

item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo.
Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a playoffs el pasado domingo, luego de que los Bravos de Atlanta ayudaran venciendo a los Astros de Houston.
Los Medias Rojas no pudieron celebrar con un triunfo en el bolsillo. Cayeron ante Tampa Bay en el último de la serie en Tropicana Field, pero eso poco importó, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta todo el camino recorrido para anotar su nombre en la fiesta de octubre luego de estar destinados al desastre en los primeros tres meses de zafra. Sencillamente nunca se rindieron, y eso lo reconoce Willson y se lo hace ver a sus compañeros.
«Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido»
«Primeramente, darle las gracias a Dios por todo lo vivido este año. Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido», dijo Willson a El Extrabase durante la celebración en el clubhouse visitante del Tropicana Field. «También hay que agradecer por el equipo que tenemos alrededor, los muchachos, la clase de personas que tenemos. Y de verdad que nunca dejamos de trabajar, ni de perseguir ese cupo a los playoffs».
En un buen tramo de la campaña, el primera base carabobeño comandó a la ofensiva patirroja. Primeramente, despuntó bateando por encima de .300 en abril y luego mantuvo la constancia suficiente como para terminar encabezando al equipo —con seis compromisos por disputar en el calendario regular— en cuadrangulares (27), carreras impulsadas (81), porcentaje de embasado (.387), slugging (.518) y OPS (.905).
Su escolta en el renglón de vuelacercas fue Wilyer Abreu (24), que no solo aportó con el bate, sino con su prodigiosa defensa en los jardines que lo tiene como firme candidato a obtener su tercer guante de oro consecutivo.
Elogios para Abreu y Monasterio
«Estoy orgulloso de todos mis compañeros, especialmente de Wilyer; por todo lo que ha hecho este año y lo que ha logrado, ha sido bastante importante, igual que (Andruw) Monasterio, que lo trajeron para acá a hacer un trabajo. Se amoldó muy bien a su rol y mira, esto es lo que hace un equipo unido, clasificar», añadió.
«Estoy verdaderamente orgulloso del equipo que formamos y que tenemos ahora mismo», acotó Wilyer, que comanda a los jardineros derechos de la Liga Americana en Carreras Salvadas a la Defensiva con 26. «Le dimos la vuelta a la temporada de una forma increíble. Me siento orgulloso de haber sido parte de esto, de poder ayudar y contribuir al equipo en este momento y durante toda la temporada».
Wilyer también destaca entre los jugadores de su posición en el nuevo circuito siendo segundo en Outs Por Encima del Promedio (3) y primero en valor en carreras de fildeo (5). Igualmente, despunta en asistencias desde los jardines (12) y en el apartado ofensivo, lidera a los Medias Rojas en carreras anotadas (81), dobles (36, con lo que comanda la Liga Americana) y bases por bolas (70). El zuliano estableció topes personales en las categorías ofensivas antes mencionadas, además de traídas al plato (74), imparables (144) y, por supuesto, bambinazos (24).
Monasterio ha entendido su rol
Por su parte, Andruw Monasterio supo adaptarse a su rol de pelotero de reemplazo, con tramos destacados a la ofensiva. Un ejemplo de ello fue julio. En ese entonces asumió la titularidad de las paradas cortas en ausencia del lesionado Trevor Story, lo que coincidió con la racha de 15 triunfos seguidos que le dio vida a Boston. Exhibió un promedio de .338 (de 65-22), OBP de .413, slugging de .631 y OPS de 1.044, con tres cuadrangulares, 11 producidas y nueve anotadas.
Pero no se limitó al campo corto; Monasterio también vio acción en segunda, en primera, e incluso en tercera.
«Para mí, todo fue amoldarme a mi rol», comentó Monasterio a El Extrabase. «Fui al Spring Training y me gané el puesto. Súper contento porque son cuatro años en el show y cuatro años clasificando, es una bendición. Es muy satisfactorio, porque tú trabajas mucho para esto, para este momento del año, el béisbol en octubre».
Suárez ha sido clave en el tramo final
En el renglón del pitcheo, Ranger Suárez ha sido clave en este tramo final de la zafra, luego de presentar altibajos durante gran parte del año e incluso estar en lista de lesionados después de la pausa del juego de estrellas.
En sus últimas cinco aperturas exhibe foja de 3-1 y una efectividad de 2.70 en 30 innings de labor, con 22 ponches, 12 pasaportes y un WHIP de 1.27. Todo eso ha confluido en una actuación general en su primera contienda en la Liga Americana, en la que posee un promedio de carreras limpias de 3.27 en 143.1 capítulos de trabajo a lo largo de 27 salidas.
«Contento del sacrificio que hicimos durante la temporada, especialmente por cómo empezamos», expresó el zurdo de Pie de Cuesta. «Entonces, mira lo que nos recompensó Dios, estamos en los playoffs».
A Ranger se lo ha caracterizado por ser un lanzador bastante calmado, casi imperturbable. Y bastante de eso mostró el equipo para lograr revertir su situación de inicio de temporada. «No comenzamos de la manera que queríamos, pero el talento de los muchachos es increíble. Sabíamos que le íbamos a dar vuelta a la situación».

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.

item.content:encoded:
After a promising start to the season (remember when the Rockies went 13-14 in April?), the Rockies are one loss away from their fifth straight 100-plus-loss season. That’s largely due to a 7-25 skid since Aug. 17.
With Colorado (57-99) hosting the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74) in its home finale Tuesday through Thursday, it’s hard to tune in with much optimism or interest right now. However, whether you plan on going to 20th and Blake to catch one last game or you’ll be tuning into Rockies.TV or KOA radio, here are some individual milestones and bright spots to look for in the final action at Coors Field in 2026.
Bark at the Park
With temperatures projected to be in the low 80s and high 70s, it’s a perfect time to bring out the dogs to Coors Field! Both Tuesday’s and Wednesday’s games will feature canines of all shapes and sizes participating in the pre-game parade for the annual Bark at the Park games. Regardless of what’s happening on the field, it’s aways fun to see the Simba Cam and how Ryan Spilborghs will interact with the dogs and fans in the stands.
K-Free’s final start as a Rockie at Coors?
131 Games over 10 seasons.
687 innings pitched.
Through the ups and downs, Kyle Freeland has been there for the Rockies. In those 131 games at Coors Field, which include 128 starts, Freeland has gone 40-40 with a 4.97 ERA and 538 strikeouts.
When he takes the mound on Tuesday against the Diamondbacks, it’s possible that it could be his last start as a Rockie at Coors Field. While Freeland, 33, has certainly had his share of struggles this year and in his career, this season he’s recorded four quality starts, including the first complete game in his career — an 8-1 win over Kansas City in the Mile High City on Aug. 2.
This season marks the end of Freeland’s five-year, $64.5 million deal. His future is unknown, and he could certainly be re-signed to stay with his hometown team. The majority of the Purple Row community believes that will be the case. Either way, it’s worth noting the history that might happen on Tuesday.
McCarthy’s triples and on-base streak
One of the most fun and exciting additions to the 2026 Rockies has been Jake McCarthy. Not only has he stepped up to be a great leadoff hitter, but his speed and ability to come up with clutch hits have made the Rockies a bigger threat at the plate.
The first thing to watch with McCarthy is to see if he can continue his on-base streak through the final homestand. McCarthy has currently reached base 22 games in a row, which is a career high for the former Diamondback. What a way to show the team that traded him what they are missing by stretching that to 25 games?
McCarthy hit a triple on Sunday against Seattle to extend his 22-game streak.
The 13th three-bagger of the year is currently the second-most in MLB behind Arizona’s Corbin Carroll, who has 16. McCarthy’s 13 triples are one shy of tying Charlie Blackmon (2017) for the second-most in a single season and only two behind Dexter Fowler’s single-season franchise best 15 in 2010. Nine of McCarthy’s triples have come at home this season. In an even deeper dive, McCarthy’s six triples during his 22-game on-base streak make him the third Rockie with six or more triples in a 22-game span in franchise history, joining Fowler (2011 and 2012) and Juan Uribe (2001).
The final thing to watch is McCarthy’s batting average. Entering the Arizona series, McCarthy is batting .297, which ranks No. 8 in MLB and No. 6 in the National League. Maybe McCarthy can take advantage of the spacious outfield at Coors Field by adding a triple or two and increasing his batting average.
Rumfield’s 24-game streak, AVG and OBP
Perhaps it’s fitting that during the same season that Todd Helton’s statue was unveiled at 20th and Blake, the Rockies seem to have found their first baseman of the future. Rumfield has proved to be the hitter the Rockies needed as a tough out who always finds a way to get on base.
Rumfield drew his 71st walk of the season to extend his on-base streak to 24 games on Sunday. On Saturday, Rumfield went 2-for-4 with an RBI and one run scored to help the Rockies beat Seattle 5-3.
Rumfield’s 24 games is the longest active streak in the Majors. It is also the longest on-base streak by a Rockie since Tyler Freeman’s 25-game streak, June 13-July 12, 2025.
Going into Tuesday, Rumfield is batting .300./.392/.451 with 71 walks and 85 strikeouts. His batting average is No. 7 in MLB and No. 5 in the National League, while his OBP is third-best in MLB and second in the National League behind Milwaukee’s Jake Bauers (.397). His numbers put him into tiers with veteran All-Stars like Jordan Alvarez and Luis Arraez, which is all the more impressive considering he’s a rookie. If he can finish hitting above .300, it will be the first time for a Rockie since Nolan Arenado (.315) and Trevor Story (.314) did it in 2019.
Then take McCarthy and Rumfield together. They are the first pair of Rockies to have an active on-base streak of at least 20 games at the same time since Charlie Blackmon (22g) and Elehuris Montero (26g) in 2023.
Goodman reaching the 40-HR milestone
Last season, Goodman had an outstanding year with 31 homers, 91 RBIs and hitting .278/.323/.520 in his first All-Star campaign. This season, he returned to the All-Star Game and enters the final homestand hitting .245/.312/.528 with 39 homers and 82 RBIs.
It would be so fitting for Goodman to hit his 40th home run at Coors Field to close out 2026. If he can hit the 40-HR milestone, whether it’s at home or in the final series of 2026 at the Chicago White Sox, Goodman will become the first Rockie to hit 40 homers since Arenado hit 41 in 2019.
It might be a long shot for Goodman to hit his 40th at Coors Field since only 16 of his 39 have come at home. But anything could happen, especially considering No. 39 came on Sunday vs. the Mariners, even though it was his first Coors Field homer since Aug. 1 vs. Kansas City.
Final thoughts
Despite the Rockies going out with a whimper instead of a bang, the end of a season can be a bittersweet feeling as it’s never fun when baseball is over. With 100 losses seeming unavoidable, at least there are some smaller, individual things to watch for.
What are you excited about in the final three games at Coors this season? Anything you’re hoping to see? Let us know in the comments!

Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.content:encoded:
Even us ‘90s kids have seen some bad Detroit Tigers teams over the years, though few have been more disappointing than the 2026 club.
Not only were the Tigers expected to compete for another AL Central crown, but they were considered a dark horse team to win their first pennant since 2012. Instead, Sunday’s 8-1 loss to the rival White Sox ended any outside hopes of A.J. Hinch’s club making its third consecutive playoff appearance.
With six games left, the 73-83 Tigers will at least avoid hitting the 90-loss mark. That’s not much of a consolation, though, and many of the team’s veterans shoulder the blame for an ugly season in the Motor City. Did you know that the Tigers’ Pythagorean win-loss record is 85-71 entering Monday?
In a decision that might generate debate, we’ve omitted Justin Verlander from this list. The expectations for him shouldn’t have been overly high, and he’s fought hard to recover from hip and hamstring problems. He’s expected to make his final MLB appearance against the Pirates this coming weekend, and we expect a heartwarming atmosphere around Comerica Park.
Should Detroit Tigers fans blame Scott Harris for the team’s disappointing 2026 season?
Objectively speaking, most of Harris’ notable moves haven’t entirely backfired. Kevin McGonigle fell to Detroit in the 2023 draft’s second round, and he’s widely expected to be the AL Rookie of the Year recipient. Veteran second baseman Gleyber Torres has been solid when he’s been healthy over the last two years, and we won't even hold the Verlander signing against Harris.
We must also reiterate that Harris inherited Javier Báez, who has indisputably been one of the worst free agent signings in Tigers history. And although he drew significant pushback for the seemingly underwhelming return for Tarik Skubal, the early returns haven’t been awful on the Tigers’ end.
Top outfield prospect Zyhir Hope has an .822 OPS in nearly 150 plate appearances at Double-A Erie, and we’ll see whether he contends for an Opening Day spot next spring. River Ryan will make his Tigers debut when he starts against the Nationals on Monday night, though Brady Scott has missed much of the last month-plus with an arm injury.
We’ve seen far worse performances by lead baseball executives this year, and Harris shouldn’t warrant being the scapegoat. But you know what they say about deserving…
Framber Valdez, SP
The most significant black mark against Valdez is his three-year, $115 million contract. Had he been a veteran who’d signed a two-year deal worth $30 million, it’d have been easy for the Tigers to accept his 4.06 ERA and diminished strikeout rate. By no means would they have been encouraged heading into 2027, but the context of someone’s salary matters.
Valdez is due nearly $43 million next season and has a $35 million player option for 2028. We'd be shocked if he doesn't opt into the latter year, but could the Tigers possibly dump his salary elsewhere? Probably not, seeing as he also has a $40 million mutual option for 2029.
When you factor in Valdez’s suspension for allegedly throwing at Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story and the subsequent accusations of immaturity, we’re not exactly optimistic about how he’ll fare next year.
Javier Báez, SS/CF
How bad has Báez been in a Tigers uniform, you ask? He's managed just 0.8 bWAR since the start of 2023, and he has a .606 OPS in that time. Across a full 162-game season, the three-time All-Star would have averaged 12 home runs, 69 RBIs, a .262 on-base percentage, and 0.3 bWAR.
This year has been a complete disaster, with an ankle problem costing Báez several months on the injured list. He’s provided Detroit with -0.8 bWAR in nearly 200 plate appearances, and his five walks against 38 strikeouts aren’t exactly encouraging about what lies ahead.
If Báez still has any diehard fans, please step up to the podium. He has one year left on his contract, and his $24 million salary might guarantee he remains in Detroit for the foreseeable future.
Matt Vierling, CF
Vierling lacks the kind of lucrative contract that Valdez and Báez signed, but he’s right alongside the latter among the team’s lowest bWAR scores. The 30-year-old center fielder managed -0.9 bWAR and a .590 OPS in 291 plate appearances before groin and heel injuries prematurely ended his season.
At this point, we’re not sure why Harris — or his potential replacement — would keep Vierling around. He's been worth -1.1 bWAR in only 122 games since the start of last year, so claiming that he lacks value is the understatement of the month.
Zach McKinstry, RF/SS
Of the four players on our list, McKinstry leads the pack with 1.5 bWAR through 124 games. It's too bad that he's managed only 26 RBIs and a .584 OPS across 366 plate appearances. How do you have such a low RBI total with that many plate appearances? Even the argument about him usually hitting no higher than sixth doesn’t work, because we’ve seen plenty of No. 7 hitters have at least 60 RBIs.
Assuming that the Tigers plan to upgrade their outfield this winter, keep your eye on the Yankees’ Trent Grisham; the two-time Gold Glove winner played this year on the qualifying offer, and Detroit might be desperate enough in hoping he can replicate his 34 homers from last season.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are headed back to the postseason, but their work is not finished. Boston enters the final week of the regular season at 84-72 after Sunday’s 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. The Red Sox secured their second consecutive postseason appearance when other results around the American League eliminated the remaining path for them to fall out of the playoff field.
The final six games will determine how prepared Boston looks when October begins. All six will be played at Fenway Park.
The Red Sox host the Cleveland Guardians at 6:45 p.m. ET on Tuesday, 7:10 p.m. Wednesday and 6:45 p.m. Thursday. Boston will conclude the regular season with three games against the Chicago Cubs from Friday through Sunday. Cleveland arrives with its own postseason urgency. The Guardians are attempting to protect their position from the Chicago White Sox, who remain close behind in the standings.
The Cubs enter the week at 87-69 after defeating the Cincinnati Reds 9-1. Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run Sunday and has emerged as one of the most dangerous power-speed players in the National League.
Trying To Get Right With The Bats
Boston’s most immediate assignment is restoring its offense. The Red Sox managed only six hits during Sunday’s loss to Tampa Bay. Trevor Story prevented a shutout with a ninth-inning home run, but Boston wasted its best opportunity after loading the bases in the fifth inning.
Roman Anthony struck out to end that threat. Patrick Sandoval allowed five runs, although he recovered from a four-run first inning to complete seven frames. The loss dropped Boston to 84-72.
Chad Tracy must use the final week to balance two priorities.
The Red Sox need enough intensity to sharpen their offense and settle any remaining pitching questions. They also cannot afford to exhaust or injure important players immediately before the postseason.
Bullpen Questions
The bullpen hierarchy is another issue. Close games against Cleveland and Chicago can function as postseason rehearsals, allowing Tracy to test his preferred late-inning combinations before every decision becomes potentially season-ending.
The Red Sox cannot catch Tampa Bay in the American League East, and the New York Yankees remain ahead of Boston in second place. That makes the final six games less about chasing a division championship and more about playoff positioning, health and momentum.
Boston already possesses its October invitation. The final week will determine what kind of team arrives.

Red Sox avanza a playoffs
Roman Anthony: "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos"
Boston es el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial, desde 1903
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida.- . "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos", dijo Roman Anthony en medio de la celebración de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por su pase a la postemporada.
Mientras los Boston Red Sox celebraban su improbable clasificación a la postemporada en el Tropicana Field, con champán y cerveza a raudales, la música del vestuario parecía la más apropiada.
"Stayin' Alive".
"Creo que eso lo dice todo", declaró el jardinero izquierdo Roman Anthony el domingo, de acuerdo a un reporte de ESPN.
El 24 de junio, los Red Sox tenían un récord de 32-46 y estaban a 15 juegos y medio del liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Desde entonces, han logrado un récord de 52-25 y se clasificarán para los playoffs.
Los Red Sox perdieron 5-1 contra los Tampa Bay Rays en el último partido de su serie, por lo que no pudieron asegurar su pase. Sin embargo, aproximadamente una hora después de que terminara el partido, los Houston Astros perdieron 4-2 contra los Atlanta Braves, lo que permitió a los Red Sox asegurar su lugar como comodín.
Poco después de que se confirmara el resultado del partido Astros-Braves, los jugadores, entrenadores y personal de los Red Sox se reunieron cerca del montículo del Tropicana Field para una foto de equipo.
"Realmente no me importa cómo entramos, lo importante es que entramos", dijo el campocorto Trevor Story.
Los Red Sox son el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial (desde 1903). Dos de los tres casos anteriores llegaron a la Serie Mundial, con los Boston Braves ganándola en 1914.
El manager interino Chad Tracy estuvo al mando durante gran parte de la remontada de este año. Desde su nombramiento el 26 de abril tras el despido de Alex Cora, los Red Sox tienen un récord de 74-55.
"Miren, no estábamos en una buena situación", dijo Tracy. "No estábamos jugando bien. Pero esto demuestra que si uno persevera, pueden suceder cosas buenas. No podría estar más orgulloso de este grupo".
El primera base Willson Contreras dijo que mantuvo la fe, incluso cuando las cosas iban mal, y la recompensa fue dulce.
“Es difícil no emocionarse hasta las lágrimas”, dijo Contreras. “Es un gran logro, pero no quiero que este equipo se detenga aquí. Quiero seguir adelante. Hemos demostrado que se puede estar en racha y superar grandes obstáculos”.
